nameStory: Green alder gets its name from the distinctive green color of its young twigs and bark, which sets it apart from its gray-barked relatives. The word 'alder' comes from the Old English 'alor,' related to the Latin 'alnus,' referring to this ancient group of water-loving trees and shrubs.
description: Green alder is a small deciduous tree or large shrub that typically grows 10-20 feet tall in New England. It has a bushy, multi-stemmed growth habit with smooth, greenish bark on younger branches that becomes gray-brown with age. Like other alders, it produces distinctive catkins (dangling flower clusters) in early spring and small woody cones that persist through winter.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Young twigs and branches have smooth, greenish bark that feels almost waxy to the touch - this green coloring is the species' signature feature

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval leaves with pointed tips and double-toothed edges, feeling slightly rough on top but smooth underneath, arranged alternately on branches

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Male flowers hang in yellowish catkins 2-4 inches long in early spring, while female flowers form small upright clusters that smell faintly sweet

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small woody cones about half an inch long that start green and turn brown, feeling hard and papery, often persisting through winter

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Usually grows as a multi-stemmed shrub or small tree with an open, irregular crown, often forming thickets in suitable habitat

habitat: Green alder thrives in moist, cool areas throughout New England's mountains and northern regions. Look for it along stream banks, in wet meadows, and on mountain slopes, often growing with other moisture-loving plants like willows and mountain ash. It's particularly common at higher elevations where cool, humid conditions prevail.

seasonality.spring: Yellowish male catkins emerge before the leaves, creating showy displays in April and May. Fresh green bark color is most noticeable as new growth begins.
seasonality.summer: Fully leafed with green foliage and developing woody cones. The characteristic green bark color on young growth is still visible beneath the leaves.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn yellow before dropping, and mature brown cones become more apparent as foliage thins.
seasonality.winter: Bare branches clearly show the greenish bark on younger twigs, and persistent woody cones help with identification. Dormant catkin buds are visible at branch tips.

funFact: Green alder has nitrogen-fixing root nodules that actually improve soil quality wherever it grows, making it a natural soil enhancer that helps other plants thrive in its vicinity - like having a botanical fertilizer factory built right into its roots!
confusionNotes: Green alder can be confused with other alders, but its greenish bark on young growth is distinctive - gray alder has gray bark, while smooth alder typically grows in warmer, lower elevation areas. Remember: green bark equals green alder!
contextualKnowledge: You might see this species listed as Alnus viridis in older field guides or plant tags, but botanists now consider that name incorrect. The accepted scientific name is Alnus alnobetula, though both names refer to the same green-barked alder you'll find in New England's mountains.
compareHints: Green alder stands out from its New England relatives by its greenish young bark - gray alder has consistently gray bark, common alder tends to be larger and more tree-like, and smooth alder has smoother leaf undersides and prefers warmer areas. The green bark color on young growth is green alder's calling card.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England alders, grey alder is distinguished by its speckled grayish bark and multi-stemmed shrubby growth habit.
Common alder differs from gray alder by having more rounded leaves with blunt tips versus gray alder's more pointed, oval leaves.
Compared to gray alder, smooth alder has much smoother bark and forms denser thickets in wetter locations.
